section: Conflict and harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSP - Champakam, Golaknath, Kesavananda, Minerva Mills

accepted.s: Which one of the following Articles was inserted by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, in response to the constitutional issue highlighted by the Champakam Dorairajan case?
accepted.x: Article 15(4) was inserted by the First Amendment Act, 1951, to enable special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes and for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
accepted.tq: Identify the precise constitutional provision associated with the judicial controversy.

accepted.s: The First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, altered the constitutional position concerning which of the following rights in the context of the Champakam Dorairajan controversy?
o: Right to constitutional remedies under Article 32
Right to equality and non-discrimination under Article 15
Right to freedom of religion under Article 25
accepted.x: The amendment concerned Article 15, which deals with equality and non-discrimination, by inserting Article 15(4). This provision enabled special measures for specified backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
accepted.tq: Use the subject of the inserted clause to identify the affected Fundamental Right.

accepted.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. I.R. Coelho judgment as the last word on the Ninth Schedule
B. First Constitutional Amendment Act
C. Champakam Dorairajan case
D. Minerva Mills judgment
accepted.x: Champakam Dorairajan and the First Amendment belong to 1951, followed later by Minerva Mills and then I.R. Coelho in 2007. The stated sequence is therefore C, B, D, A.
accepted.tq: Anchor the sequence with the two 1951 events and place I.R. Coelho last.

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The conflict between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles contributed to the development of the basic structure doctrine.
2. The conflict raised questions concerning the limits of Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution.
3. The conflict has no connection with debates on judicial and parliamentary supremacy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect because the conflict also generated debates over judicial supremacy and parliamentary supremacy.
accepted.tq: Reject the absolute negative statement and retain the two stated constitutional consequences.

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Source or development)
 a. Fundamental Rights
 b. Directive Principles of State Policy
 c. First conflict case
 d. Last word on the Ninth Schedule

List-II (Associated reference)
 i. Ireland
 ii. United States of America
 iii. Champakam Dorairajan, 1951
 iv. I.R. Coelho, 2007

option_a: a–ii, b–i, c–iii, d–iv
option_b: a–i, b–ii, c–iii, d–iv
option_c: a–ii, b–iii, c–i, d–iv
option_d: a–iii, b–i, c–ii, d–iv
accepted.x: Fundamental Rights were drawn from the United States, while the Directive Principles were inspired by Ireland. Champakam Dorairajan was the first conflict case, and I.R. Coelho in 2007 was the last word on the Ninth Schedule.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure source pair and then verify the first-case and last-word associations.

accepted.s: Which of the following best expresses the significance of the Minerva Mills judgment in the context of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
o: It treated Directive Principles as legally irrelevant to constitutional interpretation.
It treated the balance between the two as part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
It confined constitutional amendments to matters relating to the Ninth Schedule.
It made every Directive Principle superior to every Fundamental Right without exception.
accepted.x: Minerva Mills made the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles part of the Basic Structure. It did not establish absolute supremacy for either category or limit amendments only to the Ninth Schedule.
accepted.tq: Apply the Basic Structure principle to distinguish constitutional balance from absolute supremacy.
